newsitem.title: CHINA: China forces monks to denounce Dalai Lama-monitors.
newsitem.headline: China forces monks to denounce Dalai Lama-monitors.

text.p: China is forcing monks and nuns in its deeply religious Tibet region to denounce their spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, as a serpent's head in a campaign to wipe out his influence, a Tibet monitoring group said on Friday.

Political education teams had entered monasteries and temples throughout Tibet to hammer into monks and nuns Beijing's view of the Dalai Lama as a separatist and a threat to Buddhism, the London-based Tibet Information Network (TIN) said in a statement.
"Re-education teams are carrying out three-month residencies in all Tibetan monasteries as part of a programme which began in May last year to instruct monks and nuns in patriotism," it said.

After the three months of political classes, officials would give Tibet's Buddhist clergy a test quizzing them on the four aspects of the Dalai Lama as defined by Li Ruihuan, the top official in charge of religious affairs, it said, quoting from a copy of the examination.

"The correct answer...is that the Dalai is 'the head of the serpent and the chieftain of the separatist organisation conspiring for independence for Tibet...(and) the root cause of social instability in Tibet'," it said.

Li, a standing committee member of China's powerful Politburo, had also slammed Tibet's exiled god-king as a tool of foreign forces opposed to China and the biggest obstacle to the normal development of Tibetan Buddhism, it said.

Beijing has tried to weaken the influence of the Dalai Lama, worshipped as a god-king in deeply devout Tibet, with propaganda campaigns blasting him as a separatist and by banning the display of his photograph.
Previous crackdowns on religious activity in Tibet have led to occasional violence in the remote mountainous region, with monks and nuns staging riots and government buildings damaged by bombings.

Many clergy had resisted the latest campaign by refusing to take part in the classes, walking out of monasteries or declaring support for the exiled Dalai Lama, who fled Tibet in 1959 after an abortive uprising against communist rule, TIN said.
Police had arrested at least one monk in mid-June after he put up posters declaring support for the Dalai Lama and Tibetan independence, it said.
Officials had locked monks at another monastery inside the temple buildings after they refused to denounce the Dalai Lama, it said.
"The...monks were reportedly told that they would be allowed out only if they agreed to sign the patriotic education declarations," it said.

Chinese officials and media regularly accuse the Dalai Lama of seeking to split Tibet from the rest of China, and have tried to discredit the top monk, who has sought support for his cause in many Western nations.

The Dalai Lama, who won the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize for his non-violent campaign for more autonomy for his homeland, denies he is seeking Tibetan independence but says he wants a higher degree of self-government for the region's 2.4 million people.
